body:
What was the Second Urbanization?

The Second Urbanization refers to the renewed growth of towns and cities in the Indian subcontinent, particularly from around the 6th century BCE. Its main centre was the middle Ganga valley, especially parts of present-day eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

The first major phase of urbanization had occurred during the Harappan Civilization, principally in the Indus region during the 3rd millennium BCE. After the decline of the large Harappan cities, urban development took a different course. Many communities lived in villages, depended on agriculture and pastoralism, and gradually developed more permanent territorial settlements.

From approximately 600 BCE, new towns expanded in the Ganga valley. Unlike the Harappan cities, these settlements developed in the setting of emerging territorial kingdoms, increasing agricultural production, expanding trade and new forms of political authority.

Second Urbanization: The expansion of towns and cities from approximately the 6th century BCE, particularly in the Ganga valley, associated with agricultural growth, iron technology, trade, coinage and the rise of territorial states.

From Jana to Janapada and Mahajanapada

Early Vedic society was organized around groups of people called janas. Their political and social identity was closely connected with the community or clan rather than a clearly defined territory.

As agriculture expanded and settlements became more permanent, communities developed lasting connections with particular areas of land. These territories came to be called janapadas.

The word janapada literally means the land where a jana sets its foot or settles. It therefore indicates the transition from a community-based political identity towards a territorial one.

Over time, some janapadas became larger and more powerful. By the 6th century BCE, several important territorial states were known as mahajanapadas, meaning great or large janapadas.

The transformation was gradual. Janapadas did not all become mahajanapadas at the same time, and the emergence of towns, kingdoms and new agricultural techniques varied from region to region.

Why did the Ganga valley become important?

The middle Ganga basin provided favourable conditions for agricultural and political development. Its river plains contained fertile alluvial soils, rainfall supported cultivation, and rivers supplied water and convenient routes for communication.

The growing use of iron tools helped cultivators work difficult soils and clear land where necessary. Improved agricultural techniques increased production in suitable areas. Larger food supplies could support people who were not directly engaged in farming, including artisans, traders, soldiers and officials.

Consequently, agricultural villages, market centres, towns and political capitals became increasingly connected. The rise of cities was therefore related to changes in both the economy and the organization of political power.

A period of wider historical change

The 6th century BCE was also associated with the emergence of Buddhism, Jainism and other traditions of religious and philosophical thought. These developments occurred in a society experiencing expanding settlements, changing occupations, growing political authority and debates about existing social practices.

Thus, the Second Urbanization, the rise of the mahajanapadas and the appearance of new religious movements formed interconnected developments, although none can be explained by a single cause.

Prelims focus

  • The Second Urbanization began around the 6th century BCE, especially in the middle Ganga valley.
  • The first major urban civilization was the Harappan Civilization, centred principally in the Indus region.
  • Jana means a people or clan; janapada means its settled territory.
  • Mahajanapadas were larger and more powerful territorial states.
  • The growing use of iron, agricultural surplus, towns and trade accompanied the emergence of early states.
  • Trap: Iron was already used in parts of the subcontinent before the 6th century BCE. This period saw its growing use, not its first introduction.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns', printed pp. 28–30; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapter 6, printed pp. 56–59; NIOS, History 315, Lesson 5, 'From Janapadas to Empire', printed pp. 63–64, accessed 17 November 2026.]

title: The Second Urbanization: How New Towns and States Emerged

body:
How iron tools changed agriculture

The increasing use of iron was an important development in early Indian agriculture. Iron tools had appeared in parts of the subcontinent before the mahajanapada period, but their use became more widespread during the first millennium BCE.

Two important agricultural tools were the iron axe and the iron ploughshare.

Iron axes helped people clear vegetation and work with timber. Iron ploughshares made it easier to turn heavy or clayey soils, particularly in areas where rainfall and soil conditions supported plough cultivation.

These tools helped expand cultivation and improve agricultural production in suitable regions. However, iron technology was not used equally everywhere. Local conditions continued to determine which agricultural methods were practical.

The importance of paddy transplantation

Another significant development was the increasing use of paddy transplantation in parts of the Ganga valley.

In this method, rice seedlings are first grown in a nursery or prepared area. After they reach a suitable stage, the young plants are transferred to fields containing sufficient water.

Compared with simply scattering seeds, transplantation can improve the survival of seedlings and increase the productivity of suitable rice fields.

However, transplantation requires considerable labour and reliable water availability. In early agricultural society, landless labourers and dependent workers could be employed in this demanding work.

Iron ploughshare: Helped cultivators turn difficult soils more effectively.
Paddy transplantation: Helped improve rice yields by allowing seedlings to establish before being moved to prepared fields.

How agricultural surplus supported towns

Agricultural surplus is the produce remaining after cultivators meet their immediate consumption and production needs.

When agricultural output increased, more food became available for exchange, taxation and the support of non-agricultural occupations.

Artisans could specialize in pottery, weaving, carpentry or metalworking because they did not necessarily have to produce all their own food. Traders could carry agricultural and manufactured goods to other settlements. Rulers could use collected resources to support officials, soldiers and construction activities.

This relationship helps explain why agriculture was an essential economic foundation of the mahajanapadas.

From voluntary gifts to regular taxation

Earlier rulers often depended heavily on gifts and tribute. The larger mahajanapadas required more regular and predictable sources of revenue because maintaining fortifications, armies and officials was expensive.

Taxation became an increasingly important feature of political administration.

The most important revenue source was generally agriculture. A commonly described share of agricultural produce was 1/6, known as bhaga. This was a share of produce owed to the ruler, rather than a modern tax on monetary income. It should not be treated as an unchanging rate applied in every kingdom and period.

Other obligations could include:

  • Craft production: Artisans could provide labour or goods to the ruler.
  • Animal husbandry: Herders could provide animals or animal products.
  • Trade: Goods bought, sold or transported could be subject to levies.
  • Forest resources: Communities using forests could provide forest products.

Why rulers built forts and maintained armies

Many mahajanapadas developed fortified capitals. Walls made from materials such as earth, wood, brick or stone helped protect settlements against attack.

Fortifications also demonstrated a ruler's power and made it easier to control important settlements and resources.

As political competition increased, some states developed standing armies maintained through regular revenue. Others continued to depend partly on soldiers mobilized when required.

The relationship between production and political authority was therefore reciprocal. Agricultural resources supported the state, while rulers sought to protect territories, control routes and collect revenue.

Prelims focus

  • Iron axes helped clear vegetation; iron ploughshares helped cultivate difficult soils.
  • Paddy transplantation increased the survival of seedlings in suitable rice-growing areas.
  • Bhaga was commonly described as 1/6 of agricultural produce.
  • Mahajanapadas collected taxes to support armies, officials and fortifications.
  • Agricultural surplus helped support artisans, traders and urban populations.
  • Trap: Not every mahajanapada had an identical tax system or a permanent standing army.

[NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapter 6, 'Kingdoms, Kings and an Early Republic', printed pp. 57–60; Chapter 9, 'Vital Villages, Thriving Towns', printed pp. 87–89; NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, printed pp. 29–31 and 38–39; NIOS, History 315, Lesson 5, printed pp. 63–64, accessed 17 November 2026.]

title: Iron, Agriculture and the Economic Foundations of Early States

body:
The growth of early historic towns

From approximately the 6th century BCE, towns expanded in several parts of the subcontinent. Many were associated with the capitals of mahajanapadas, while others developed as important commercial and cultural centres.

Examples of important early towns include Rajagriha, Vaishali, Shravasti, Varanasi, Kaushambi and Ujjayini. Mathura was also an important centre because of its position along major routes. Pataliputra became especially prominent as Magadha developed into a larger state.

These towns served several functions. Rulers and officials administered territories from political centres. Traders exchanged goods. Craftspeople produced articles for local and distant markets. Religious teachers and their followers also gathered in important settlements.

Why trade routes influenced the location of towns

Transporting goods was easier where settlements had access to reliable communication routes.

Rivers such as the Ganga and Yamuna provided important routes for carrying goods and people. Land routes connected agricultural regions, political capitals and commercial centres.

Important commercial connections linked places such as Varanasi, Kaushambi, Shravasti, Mathura and Taxila. Routes through Mathura also connected northern India with Ujjayini and western India.

Rulers had an interest in controlling such routes because trade supported economic activity and could generate revenue.

Craft specialization in towns

Urban growth created demand for goods made by specialized producers. These included:

  • Potters producing household vessels and fine pottery.
  • Blacksmiths making iron tools and other metal objects.
  • Weavers producing cloth.
  • Carpenters making wooden articles and equipment.
  • Goldsmiths and other metalworkers producing ornaments.

One notable ceramic type associated with many early historic settlements was Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW). It was generally fine pottery with a hard, glossy, often black surface. Such vessels were probably used by relatively prosperous groups.

NBPW should be distinguished from Painted Grey Ware (PGW), which is associated with several earlier settlements and is characterized by grey pottery with painted designs, often geometric patterns.

What were shrenis?

As production and commerce became more organized, many artisans and merchants formed associations called shrenis, commonly described as guilds.

Craft guilds could arrange training, acquire raw materials and organize the distribution of finished products. Merchant guilds helped organize commercial activities.

In the wider early historic period, some shrenis also received deposits and supported religious institutions through financial arrangements.

A shreni was therefore an association connected with production or commerce, not a territorial state or a political assembly.

The introduction of punch-marked coins

The expansion of trade was accompanied by the use of coins. Among the earliest coin types in the subcontinent were punch-marked coins, appearing from approximately the 6th century BCE onwards.

These coins were generally made of silver, although copper examples also existed. They are called punch-marked because symbols were stamped or punched onto pieces of metal.

Early punch-marked coins did not normally carry the portrait of a ruler. Their symbols could include various geometric or recognizable designs.

Coins helped facilitate exchange, but their introduction did not mean that every transaction used money. Direct exchange of goods and other forms of payment continued.

Punch-marked coins: Early coins bearing stamped symbols, commonly made of silver.
Shreni: An association of artisans or merchants.
NBPW: Fine pottery with a characteristic glossy surface, associated with many early historic settlements.

Trade connections with Gujarat

Commercial routes connected the Ganga valley with central and western India. Mathura served as a point of connection towards Ujjayini and coastal regions, including present-day Gujarat.

This provides a relevant Gujarat connection to the broader economic developments of the period. However, the presence of western trade routes does not mean that a state centred in present-day Gujarat was included among the conventional sixteen mahajanapadas.

Prelims focus

  • Many early towns were capitals of mahajanapadas or centres of trade.
  • Northern Black Polished Ware is associated with early historic towns.
  • Shrenis were associations of craftspeople or merchants.
  • Early punch-marked coins were generally made of silver; copper examples also existed.
  • Mathura was connected with major routes leading towards northern, central and western India.
  • Trap: Punch-marked coins were not generally portrait coins, and their use did not eliminate barter.

[NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, 2018–19, Chapter 9, 'Vital Villages, Thriving Towns', printed pp. 87–94; NCERT, Themes in Indian History Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, 'Kings, Farmers and Towns', printed pp. 42–45; NIOS, History 315, Lesson 5, 'From Janapadas to Empire', printed pp. 63–64, accessed 17 November 2026.]
